passage: I'm Tara, and my desk faces the small meeting corner where Ishita meets Dilnaz on Wednesdays. Last week Dilnaz arrived stuck on a slow report page. I expected Ishita to type the fix. Instead Ishita asked, 'What have you tried?' Dilnaz listed two things. 'What else could it be?' Dilnaz named three options, hesitating. 'And if you chose the second one, how might it go wrong?' Dilnaz went quiet, then said, 'It could hide the real problem.' Ishita nodded and asked which option to test first. Twenty minutes later Dilnaz was typing alone. I can't say whether it felt frustrating or exciting to Dilnaz, but Dilnaz left with the answer and a small grin.

qa.q: How many options did Dilnaz name?
What might Dilnaz have been feeling when going quiet?
qa.a: Dilnaz was possibly uncertain and concentrating hard, and the small grin at the end suggests some satisfaction.

qa.q: What could Ishita do if Dilnaz stayed stuck?
qa.a: Ishita could give a small hint about where to look, without solving it, since a nudge keeps the thinking with Dilnaz.

qa.q: How might Tara have seen Ishita's way of helping?
qa.a: Tara expected a typed fix, so was probably surprised and interested in how much Dilnaz did alone.

grounding: Shows a mentor asking what has been tried, what the options are and how each might fail so the mentee reasons through the problem.

subtype: Approach: asking questions to build thinking [Thinking]
passage:
Monday. Pooja arrives at Arohi's desk with a failing test. 'Just tell me what's wrong.' Arohi pulls up a chair but keeps her hands in her lap. 'What have you tried so far?' Pooja lists two things. 'What else could it be?' Pooja guesses three more. 'How would each one fail?' Forty minutes later, Pooja finds it herself: a time-zone bug.
Thursday. Another problem, a slow page. Pooja writes on a notepad before coming over: what I tried, three options, how each might fail. Arohi asks only one question. Pooja goes back and fixes it.
The next Wednesday. Pooja doesn't come to Arohi's desk at all. Instead she messages: 'Found a memory leak. Tried two things, the third one worked. Wrote it up for the team.' Arohi reads it twice and smiles.

qa.q: What bug did Pooja find on Monday?
What does Arohi's smile on Wednesday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Arohi feels proud and pleased that Pooja can now reason through problems alone.

qa.q: Why did Arohi keep her hands in her lap on Monday?
qa.a: To make Pooja think through the options instead of watching a fix, so the reasoning becomes Pooja's own.

qa.q: How did Pooja's experience change over the week?
qa.a: Pooja moved from wanting an answer to arriving with options, and finally solved a problem alone and shared it with the team.

grounding: It shows a mentor asking what has been tried, what the options are and how each might fail, guiding the mentee to reason through problems.

subtype: Approach: asking questions to build thinking [Thinking]
passage: Nikita, you asked how to mentor your first junior. Let your Aadhya Didi tell you about mine. I was twenty-four, stuck on a database migration, and I went to Mr Menon expecting an answer. He gave me three questions instead. What have you tried? What are all the options? How might each one fail? I was annoyed. I wanted him to just tell me. But I answered, and halfway through the third question, I saw my own mistake: I'd planned to migrate everything at once, and it would have locked the system for hours. He hadn't said a word about it. Twenty years later, I still ask myself those three questions before every big change. So when your junior comes to you, don't hand over the solution. Hand over the questions.

qa.q: What three questions did Mr Menon ask?
qa.a: What have you tried? What are all the options? How might each one fail?

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when Mr Menon gave questions instead of an answer?
qa.a: She was annoyed at first, wanting a quick answer, before discovering her own mistake.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aadhya's story?
qa.a: Answering the third question and spotting, without being told, that migrating everything at once would lock the system.

qa.q: How might Mr Menon have seen that conversation?
qa.a: He likely felt quietly satisfied seeing Aadhya find the mistake herself, which is why he said nothing about it.

grounding: It shows a mentor asking what has been tried, what the options are and how each might fail, guiding the mentee to reason through the problem.
